text: Git is a trustworthy source of truth, but something still has to get changes from that repo onto a live cluster. There are two fundamentally different ways to do that, and the direction the connection runs turns out to matter enormously for security. This lesson walks through why.

Here's the push model most teams start with. The deploy stage in a CI pipeline runs az aks get-credentials to fetch a kubeconfig, then kubectl apply straight against production. For this to work, the CI system has to hold credentials privileged enough to modify a live cluster, decrypted into the runner's memory on every run, with the cluster's API server reachable from wherever that runner lives.

That's a real liability, not a theoretical one. A leaked secret, a poisoned dependency in a build step, or a malicious pull request that gets CI to run arbitrary code can all expose or abuse those same privileged credentials. And scoping them tightly per app and per environment is tedious enough that most teams don't bother, so the blast radius of one compromise is often the whole cluster. On top of that, the API server has to accept inbound connections from CI at all, which fights against keeping it on a private network.

GitOps inverts the direction entirely. An agent running inside the cluster — Argo CD and Flux are the real examples — watches Git and pulls changes toward itself, authenticating outbound with a read-only deploy key, then applying them with its own in-cluster RBAC. No external system ever holds a cluster-admin credential, and no inbound connection to the API server is needed for deployment at all.

That's the OpenGitOps principle Pulled Automatically: software agents pull desired state from the source, rather than a pipeline pushing it in. CI's job shrinks to building, testing, and updating Git; it never touches the cluster again. Next lesson covers what that in-cluster agent does continuously once it's watching — specifically, how it catches and corrects drift.
